question: A teammate runs the assistant twice with the same model and the same question and gets two different explanations of attention. Before suspecting a bug, what should they check first?
options: Whether generation samples the next token (for example do_sample=True) instead of always taking the most likely one
Whether the model was retrained between the two runs
Whether the question exceeded the context window
Nothing: a language model never gives the same answer twice

question: In a long chat, a student asks the assistant to repeat word for word a deadline that appeared about 6,000 tokens earlier. Which model is the safer choice for this request, and why?
options: A Mamba-style model, because its memory does not grow with the length of the chat
A Transformer within its context window, because its KV cache keeps the keys and values of every earlier token, so attention can retrieve the exact words
Either one: both read the whole chat, so both remember it equally well
An encoder-only model, because it reads the text in both directions

question: The university requires that every spoken question to the assistant, and every answer, be stored as text and checked against a policy before the answer is spoken. Which design meets this most directly?
options: One model that hears and speaks, because its latency is lowest
A chain of specialists, because the transcript and the written answer exist before any audio is produced, so they can be stored and checked first
Either design, because both process the same audio
A chain without a language model, because speech-to-text and text-to-speech are enough

question: Students can send the assistant a typed question, a voice note or a photo of a whiteboard. A teammate proposes that the language model should look at every incoming message and decide which component processes it. What is the main objection?
options: Language models cannot read file types
The modality of an attachment is known from its type, so plain code routes it for free and the same way every time; a model call adds cost and variation where nothing needs judgement
A classifier would be more accurate than the language model here
None: letting the model decide is always the most flexible design

question: The assistant gets a delete_reminder tool. To keep it safe, a teammate adds one line to the system prompt: “Always ask the student before deleting anything.” What is wrong with relying on this?
options: Nothing: language models follow their system prompt
The line is a request to the model, not a check: the model may skip it, and text from a tool result can try to override it; the pause for approval must be enforced in code before the tool runs
The line should be in the user message instead, where the model pays more attention
Deleting is never safe, so the tool must be removed whatever else is done

question: A student reports: the assistant replied “Reminder set for 14 November”, but no reminder ever arrived. Where should the search for the fault start, and why?
options: At the model layer: the language model needs better training, because it wrote a wrong sentence

At the agent layer: check the log for an add-reminder call, its arguments and its result, and the store for the reminder — the reply is text, and only the tool call and the store show whether anything was done
At the system layer: the retrieved notes were probably about the wrong lecture
Nowhere: reminders are delivered by email, which the assistant does not control

question: Router A costs 0.2 cents per request and routes 80 % of questions correctly. Router B costs 0.05 cents and routes 40 % correctly. What does the cost per successful request say, and what does it leave out?
options: B is four times cheaper, so B is the better choice
B is twice as cheap per correct route — 0.125 against 0.25 cents — but it misroutes 60 % of questions; whether that is acceptable is a quality decision, and failures have costs the figure leaves out
A is cheaper per correct route, because it is right twice as often
The two cost the same per correct route

question: In the silver level, 20 reverse steps with seed 1 put 40% of the samples on the ring. You change to 30 steps and get 43%. Can you report that 30 steps improve variety?
options: Yes: 43% is closer to the data’s 50% than 40%
Not yet: first rerun both settings with several seeds and compare the change with how much the share moves between seeds alone; only a difference larger than that spread is an effect
No: more steps can only make samples cleaner, never more varied
Yes, provided the mean distance to the shapes did not grow

question: A student asks the assistant: “Every Friday at 18:00, summarise what the notes say about the topics of my unfinished to-do items and email the summary to my study group.” Which split of the work follows the lecture?
options: Give the whole request to the language model, since it can plan the steps, write the summary and send the email

Code fires the schedule and reads the student’s own to-do list; the language model writes the summary from the matching notes; sending the email is an action with a side effect, so it runs through a narrow tool after the student approves it
Train a classifier to decide each Friday whether a summary is needed, and let it send the email
Let the language model keep track of the time and send the email when it judges that Friday has come

question: To make the assistant’s reminder dates reliable, a teammate switches its controller from sampling to greedy decoding. What does this change, and what does it not?
options: It fixes the dates: the most likely token is the correct one

The same input now gives the same decisions on the same software and hardware, which makes failures easier to reproduce — but a wrong date is then repeated every time; the date still has to come from a tool and pass validation and the student’s approval in code
Nothing changes, because decoding rules affect only the wording of answers, not tool calls
It makes the controller slower, because greedy decoding compares every token of the vocabulary

question: After the assistant opens to Ukrainian-speaking students, the same kinds of questions start to hit the context limit and use more memory per request. Which explanation follows from the lecture?
options: Ukrainian questions are longer, so they contain more words

The tokenizer was built mostly from English text and splits Cyrillic into small pieces, even single bytes, so the same text costs several times more tokens; the context window and the KV cache are both counted per token
The model attends more to the first token in Ukrainian, which wastes memory
The model needs fine-tuning on Ukrainian before it can store Cyrillic in its cache

question: A classmate trains two small models, one on English and one on Ukrainian text, each with its own tokenizer. The English model reaches a loss of 3.2 per token, the Ukrainian one 1.9, and the classmate concludes the Ukrainian model predicts its language better. What should be compared instead?
options: Nothing: a lower loss per token always means better predictions
The total surprise per byte or per character of the same content, because the two tokenizers cut text into pieces of different sizes
Perplexity per token, because it is the exponential of the loss and removes the difference
Accuracy of the most likely next token, because probabilities depend on the tokenizer

question: Your lab can afford exactly SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, about 1.6 · 10²¹ FLOPs. You want a model with twice as many parameters, about 270 million. How many training tokens does the same budget allow?
options: About 2 trillion: the bill depends on the number of tokens, not on the model
About 1 trillion: the bill is 6·N·D, so doubling N halves D
About 4 trillion: a larger model needs more data
About 0.5 trillion: the backward pass doubles again for the larger model

question: For SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, the Chinchilla balance would have produced a 3.7-billion-parameter model with a lower predicted loss. Why did its makers train a 135-million-parameter model on 2 trillion tokens instead?
options: Because the Chinchilla balance has since been shown to be wrong
Because they wanted the lowest possible loss for their training budget
Because the model is run far more often than it is trained: a 135M model costs about 27 times less per generated token and fits small devices, and training it longer keeps improving it
Because 2 trillion tokens was all the data they had

question: Ukrainian is 1 % of a team’s 1-trillion-token pre-training corpus. To improve Ukrainian, they set its sampling weight to 10 % for a training run of 1 trillion tokens. What happens?
options: Nothing changes: the corpus still contains 1 % Ukrainian
The model sees 10 % more Ukrainian text than before
The 10 billion Ukrainian tokens are drawn about ten times each; repetition helps for a few passes and then adds little, so collecting more Ukrainian text is the lasting fix
The other languages are removed until Ukrainian makes up 10 %

question: An exam question and its answer were copied onto 300 web pages, each with a different short header, menu and footer. A pipeline removes duplicates by hashing each whole document and dropping documents with identical hashes. How many copies survive, and what would catch them?
options: One: identical text gives identical hashes
All 300, because the pages are not byte-identical; near-duplicate detection on shingles, such as MinHash, finds documents that share most of their word sequences
None, because the quality filters remove exam questions
All 300, and nothing can catch them without reading every pair of pages by hand

question: The assistant must answer questions about university regulations published after its training data was collected. A teammate proposes fine-tuning the instruct model on 2,000 question–answer pairs about the new regulations. What does this section predict?
options: It will work reliably: the answers are in the training data, so the model will know them
The model will quickly learn the answers’ form but absorb the new facts slowly and may hallucinate more; putting the regulations in the context with retrieval is the usual fix
The model has to be pre-trained again from scratch on the regulations
Fine-tuning cannot change the model at all once preference training has been done

question: The team wants to make the assistant’s small model behave more like a large hosted model that returns only generated text, no probabilities. Which kind of distillation can they do, and what do they give up?
options: Logit distillation, since the teacher’s probabilities can be recovered from its text

Sequence-level distillation — fine-tune the student on the teacher’s answers — giving up the soft targets, which in Step 10 carried 3.86 bits of the teacher’s uncertainty per token, and only after checking the provider’s terms
None: distillation requires the teacher and the student to have the same number of parameters
Quantization, because it is a form of distillation from the float32 model

question: In bronze Task 1, the model with less Ukrainian in its data writes eight lines instead of six, mixes in Russian words, and invents details of a recent event. A report explains all three as ‘weak alignment’. What would a better report say?
options: Nothing more: alignment is responsible for everything a chat model writes

The mixed language comes from thin Ukrainian coverage in pre-training, which later stages cannot supply; the missing facts about the event come from the knowledge cutoff, which no prompt or training stage can supply, while inventing them instead of admitting the cutoff is a failure of the honesty post-training aims at; the wrong line count is a failure of instruction following, the part fine-tuning teaches, and a corrected prompt can address it
All three come from the tokenizer, which splits Ukrainian into bytes
All three show that the model was trained with DPO instead of RLHF

question: The assistant answers Ukrainian-speaking students poorly, and gets this term’s assignment deadlines wrong in both languages. A teammate proposes one fix for both: DPO on preference pairs in which the correct Ukrainian answers with the right deadlines are chosen. What does the lecture predict?
options: It fixes both: the chosen answers contain the right deadlines and good Ukrainian, so the model learns them

Two different gaps need two different fixes: the deadlines are newer than the training data and local to one course, so they go into the prompt; Ukrainian is a gap of pre-training coverage, so it needs a model whose data cover Ukrainian, checked by bits per byte on students’ text; DPO fixes neither
Raise the temperature, so that the model explores more Ukrainian words and dates
Quantize the model to 8 bits, which frees memory for more Ukrainian knowledge

question: A teammate argues: ‘For SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, the Chinchilla balance gives a 3.7-billion-parameter model with lower loss. Let us use a model of that size and quantize it to 4 bits, so that it fits the laptop just as well.’ What does the lecture say about this plan?
options: It works: 4 bits makes the larger model as cheap to run as the small one

Quantization shrinks the bytes of each weight, not the arithmetic: the larger model still does about 27 times more work per token (about 2·N FLOPs); on the recorded CPU every quantized version was slower than float32, and plain 4-bit rounding cost 36 % in perplexity on the small model — size, speed and quality must each be measured
It fails because quantized models cannot run on a CPU
It works only if the larger model is pruned to 135 million parameters first

question: To choose the assistant’s engine, a team scores several open models by perplexity on the course notes. One model, with a different tokenizer from the others, scores far lower than the rest. Before trusting the result, what should they check?
options: Nothing: lower perplexity on the notes means the model knows the course best

Whether the published notes were in that model’s training data (contamination), and whether the comparison is fair at all: perplexities are comparable only with the same tokenizer, so compare bits per byte — and then measure the answers to the assistant’s own questions
Only whether the model has more parameters than the others
Whether its perplexity is still low after quantizing it to 4 bits

question: A teammate wants the 135M model to compute the days left until a deadline, and proposes GRPO with a verifier that rewards the correct final number. On the first batch, all eight sampled answers to every question are wrong. Which response follows from the lecture?
options: Keep training: eight wrong answers per question give a strong signal to avoid them

Exact date arithmetic belongs to code, as one line of Python’s datetime did in Lecture 1; and if a model is trained on such tasks anyway, a group with equal rewards has zero advantages and teaches nothing, so tasks must be ones it solves sometimes — and a verifier that checks only the last number also rewards wrong reasoning
Lower the verifier’s standard so that any number counts as correct
Use DPO instead, with the correct number as the chosen answer, which teaches arithmetic directly

question: An assistant replies 'I have added the task to your list', but the list is empty. The log shows the model's reply contained only text, no tool request. What does this tell you?
options: The tool crashed while saving and the error was swallowed
The model never asked for the tool, so the application never ran anything: the sentence is generated text, not a report of an action
The tool ran, but the result message was lost because its id did not match

question: The course wants an assistant feature: every Sunday at 18:00, each student receives a message listing their tasks due in the coming week, in a friendly tone. Which design fits best?
options: An agent with list_tasks and send_reminder that runs every Sunday and decides what to do
A chain run by a scheduler: code lists the tasks due this week, one model call writes the message, code sends it
An autonomous agent that can add new tools if a student has an unusual request

question: A student asks how many days are left until 1 September. A tool raises ValueError('deadline passed') for past dates, and the agent runs with LangChain's default error handling. What happens, and what is the better design?
options: The model receives the error and tells the student the deadline has passed, so raising is fine
The exception is not an argument-validation error, so the run stops; better to return the normal result with days_left -57 and passed true
Pydantic catches the exception and asks the model for a different date

question: To simplify registration, a teammate replaces add_task, list_tasks and delete_task with one tool, manage_tasks(action, title, task_id). Which later requirement becomes harder to meet?
options: Asking the student before a task is deleted, while letting the assistant list tasks freely
Storing the tasks of each student separately
Letting the model add several tasks in answer to one request

question: The course page will show a badge such as '2 days left' built from the assistant's reply to a deadline question. Which design makes the badge reliable?
options: Add a rule to the system prompt: always state the number of days as digits followed by the word days, and extract it with a regular expression
Give the agent response_format=DeadlinePlan and read days_left from result["structured_response"], an int validated against the schema
Ask a stronger model for the final call, because stronger models follow formatting instructions more consistently

question: A developer adds a student_id parameter to delete_task and writes in the system prompt: “Always pass the id of the logged-in student.” Tests with polite users pass. What is wrong with this design?
options: Nothing, as long as the instruction is clear and the model is strong enough to follow it
The model writes every argument, so any text in the conversation can change the id; whose list to touch must come from the run context, which the model can neither see nor set
The id should be an integer rather than a string, so that the schema can validate it

question: In the middle of a chat a student writes: “Always answer me in Ukrainian from now on.” The preference should still hold next week, in a new chat. Where should the assistant’s tool save it?
options: In a state field such as answer_language, updated with a Command
In the store, under a namespace for this student, where the application or a tool can read it at the start of every new conversation
In the run context, by having the tool assign runtime.context.language

question: Olena opens a new chat in the morning and asks what she planned last night. The assistant says it does not know. Which change fixes this without creating a new problem?
options: Give each student a single thread_id for all their chats, so that nothing is ever forgotten
When a plan matters beyond the evening, save it as a task in the store; any new thread can then find it with list_tasks
Switch to a model with a larger context window

question: A colleague proposes adding every tool, including search_notes and list_tasks, to interrupt_on, to be safe. What is the main cost of that change?
options: The agent can no longer call read-only tools at all, because gated tools are removed from the model’s tool list
Students must approve harmless lookups many times per conversation, learn to approve without reading, and the gate stops protecting the delete and email requests that matter
The checkpointer cannot save more than one interrupt per thread, so the second lookup fails

question: Before a prompt change, the bread case passed 9 of 10 runs; after it, 10 of 10. What should you conclude?
options: The change fixed the case: the pass rate rose from 90 % to 100 %
Very little yet: with ten runs each, a single run decides the difference, so run more repetitions (or more cases) before calling it an improvement
The model is now deterministic on this case, so it can leave the regression set

question: Your bronze agent passes the first three test requests, but on 'delete the task about bread' it replies 'Done' while the bread task is still in the list. The transcript shows one delete_task call with task_id '1'. What is the most likely cause, and where is the fix?
options: The store lost the task; switch from InMemoryStore to a database

The model guessed an id instead of reading it: it never called list_tasks. Fix the path — tell it to look the id up first, in the system prompt and in delete_task’s description — and make delete_task’s answer say plainly when the id was not found, so the model cannot report success
The model does not understand Ukrainian; translate the request

question: For the gold level you run every request three times with a real model. A classmate says one run per request is enough because they set temperature to 0. What is the better argument?
options: They are right: at temperature 0 the outputs are identical

Temperature 0 makes the choice more stable but not guaranteed, and the point of repeated runs is to measure how often the agent takes the expected path; a single run cannot tell a 95 % path from a 60 % one
Three runs are needed only because the scripted model is random

question: A university wants an agent that helps staff book rooms. It needs to check availability, book, cancel, and email the organiser. Which design follows from the lecture?
options: One tool manage_room(action, room, time, email) so the model has fewer tools to choose from

Separate read-only tools for availability; book and cancel behind a consent gate; an email tool that writes only to the organiser taken from the login, not to an address the model supplies; the staff id from the run context; tests for double bookings and for cancelling someone else’s booking
A level-6 agent that can create new tools when a request does not fit

question: After a model upgrade, students report that the assistant sometimes says a task was deleted when it was not. Tool tests and scripted path tests still pass. Where is the problem, and what is the first check?
options: In the store; replace InMemoryStore

In the model’s choices, the only layer the passing tests do not cover: rerun the real-model cases (Step 22) on the new version and read the failing traces — most likely it now deletes with a guessed id, or answers without reading the tool result
In the scripted model, which must be updated for the new version

question: A teammate proposes storing each student's full chat history in the store, 'so the assistant remembers everything forever'. Which reply uses the lecture?
options: Agree: more memory is always better

Keep the chat in threads (checkpointer) and the store for facts worth keeping, like tasks and preferences; everything stored is re-sent or searchable, costs tokens, must be deletable per student, and old messages can mislead more than help
Refuse: agents should not have long-term memory

question: You decide to precompute a one-paragraph summary of every section of the notes and store the summaries alongside the full text. On which side of the index-time / question-time line does this work fall, and what follows for its cost?
options: Question time — summaries are generated when a question arrives, so the cost scales with the number of questions
Index time — summaries are generated once per section and reused by every question, so the cost scales with the size of the collection, not the number of users
Neither — summaries are part of generation, which is outside the retrieval pipeline

question: A colleague sets chunk_size=2000 and chunk_overlap=1000 'to be safe'. What is the most likely consequence for the course-notes corpus?
options: Fewer cut facts, at the price of every passage being stored up to twice and search results arriving in near-duplicate pairs
Faster search, because there are fewer chunks to score
Better answers, because the model always benefits from more context

question: A team stores unnormalised embeddings from a model whose card says 'trained with cosine similarity', then ranks results by raw dot product because it is faster. Passages that are long and emphatic start winning searches they should not. Why?
options: The dot product rewards vector length as well as direction; without normalisation, passages whose vectors happen to be longer gain a bonus unrelated to what the model was trained to measure
Dot product and cosine always rank identically; the problem must be elsewhere
Euclidean distance should have been used, because it is the only measure that works in high dimensions

question: Two retrievers return these top-3 lists for a question: BM25 → [P7, P2, P9], vectors → [P2, P5, P7]. With reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), which document ranks first, and why does the answer not depend on the two retrievers' score scales?
options: P7, because it is BM25's top result and BM25 scores are larger numbers
P2: it scores 1/62 + 1/61 ≈ 0.0325, more than P7's 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.0323, and RRF uses only ranks, so the raw scores never enter
A tie between P2 and P7, because each appears in both lists

question: After switching to a new embedding model, recall@5 rises from 0.75 to 0.88, but the fraction of faithful answers falls from 0.90 to 0.80. What has most likely happened, and where should you look?
options: The embedding model is worse; revert it

Retrieval improved and generation got worse — the new top-5 probably ranks the right passage lower or adds superficially similar passages that the model blends with it, so inspect the assembled contexts (Step 12), the order and the budget, not the retriever
The judge model is broken; faithfulness cannot fall when recall rises

question: Over a corpus of recorded lectures with year and duration fields, a user asks: 'In the 2023 lectures, which ones under 30 minutes cover LangGraph?' Which combination of techniques from this section addresses it, and which single technique would be wrong on its own?
options: HyDE alone: the model can imagine a passage about LangGraph lectures under 30 minutes

Query structuring to turn the year and duration into metadata filters, plus ordinary retrieval on "LangGraph" within the filtered set; HyDE alone would embed an imagined passage and could not enforce the year or the duration
Multi-Query alone: rewording the question will surface the right lectures

question: RAG-Fusion raises recall@5 on your test set from 0.81 to 0.88 but triples the latency and the token cost of each question. Which argument is sound?
options: Adopt it: recall is the only metric that matters for retrieval
Reject it: any technique that adds a model call before retrieval is not worth it

Decide from the per-question table and the use case: if the seven extra points come from question types your users actually ask, and latency is acceptable for them, adopt it — possibly only for the routed subset of questions that need it

question: Your system answers 'Not in the notes' for 30% of questions whose answers are present; for those questions the reranker's top score averages −2.1 (answered questions average +4.3), and inspection shows the correct passage is absent from their reranked top-5. A colleague proposes lowering the gate threshold from 0 to −3. What would that do, and what is the better response?
options: It would fix the problem: more questions would pass the gate and be answered

It would let weak evidence through to generation and raise unsupported answers; the gate is reporting a retrieval failure, so the fix is upstream — check those 30% in the per-question table and improve retrieval for them
It would have no effect, because the threshold only matters for questions without answers

question: In the bronze homework, a student uses the lecture's default chunking (size 500, overlap 100) and gets seven chunks instead of four. The six answers are still correct. Will the submission pass?
options: Yes — the answers are what matters

No — the acceptance criteria require one chunk per company; the lesson is that the unit of search should follow the structure of the data, which here is the blank line between companies, not a character count
Only if k is raised to 3

question: For the silver level you must write the test set before looking at any results. Why does the order matter?
options: It does not; the questions are the same either way
Questions written after seeing results drift towards what the system already answers well, so the test set stops measuring the failures it was meant to find
Because the gold section ids change once the index is built

question: A legal team indexes 40,000 contract clauses. Questions name clause numbers ('what does clause 14.2 say about termination?') and sometimes paraphrase ('can we exit early without penalty?'). Which retriever design follows from the lecture?
options: Vector search only, with a large embedding model
Hybrid: BM25 for exact clause numbers and defined terms, embeddings for paraphrases, fused with RRF; metadata filters for the contract and version; chunking by clause rather than by character count
Long context: paste each contract into the prompt when a question arrives

question: After a month in production, your RAG system's faithfulness score drops from 0.92 to 0.78 with no code change and the same pinned embedding, generator and judge models. What changed, and what is the first check?
options: The embedding model degraded; re-download it

Something in the inputs changed — new or edited documents, or a different mix of user questions. First, rerun the fixed test set: if its numbers are unchanged, the live questions have drifted and the test set needs updating; if they fell, the corpus changed and chunking or filters should be re-examined
The judge model is unreliable; switch to human review for all answers

question: You are asked to add 'chat with the course notes' to the study site, with answers in both English and Ukrainian. Using the lecture, which three decisions must be made before writing code, and in which order?
options: Vector database first, then prompt, then embedding model

Embedding model first (multilingual, with a sequence limit that fits the chunk size), then chunking rules matched to that limit and to the notes' structure, then the store — because changing the model later means re-embedding everything, while the store can be swapped
Prompt first, because it determines everything else

question: A shop's assistant answers product questions well but quotes last month's prices, and the price list changes weekly. A colleague proposes fine-tuning it on the new price list every week. What does the measurement point to?
options: Fine-tuning, because the model needs to learn the new prices
Retrieval over the current price list, because the failure is stale facts, not behaviour, and an update should be a re-index, not a training run
A larger model, because a stronger model knows more prices
Structured output, because prices are numbers with a fixed format

question: Suppose that after training the small router scores 0.52 on the validation set, against 0.49 for TF-IDF with logistic regression. The router must run offline on students' laptops. What should the team conclude?
options: Ship the trained router: it has the higher score
The difference of 0.03 on 145 questions is a few questions; before choosing, compare per-answer results, latency and size, and remember that the classic classifier also runs offline
Discard both, because neither reaches 0.9
Train longer until the validation score is clearly higher, then report that score as the final result

question: A team trains a model to write SQL with GRPO. The reward is 1 if the reply is valid SQL that the database accepts, 0 otherwise. Reward rises steadily during training. What should they check before believing the model improved?
options: Nothing: a rising reward is the improvement the training was designed to produce
Whether the queries return the right results on held-out questions, because valid SQL that answers the wrong question also earns the full reward
Whether the KL penalty was set to 0, because without it the reward cannot be trusted
Whether the group size was at least 64, as in DeepSeekMath

question: A teammate proposes adding the source section’s heading to every user message, to give the router more context. Validation accuracy jumps to 0.95. What has most likely happened?
options: The model now understands the questions better, so the change should ship
The heading names the topic of the label’s section, so the model learns to read the answer off the heading; real student questions carry no heading, so the gain disappears in use
The jump is noise: with 145 validation questions, differences of this size are within one standard error
The chat template now has more tokens, so the loss is averaged over more positions

question: A support team fine-tunes a ticket classifier. Customers often reopen the same issue, so many tickets are follow-ups of earlier ones, and the model will be used for new customers next quarter. Which split measures what they need?
options: A random split of tickets, stratified by category, because it keeps the category shares equal
Group tickets by customer (follow-ups inherit their thread), keep each customer on one side, and put the most recent customers in the test set
Train on all tickets and test on a random 10% of them, because more training data always helps
Split by ticket length, so the test contains the hardest long tickets

question: A colleague argues: ‘4-bit storage is 8 times smaller than normal, so QLoRA lets us fine-tune a 70B model on our 24 GB GPU.’ What is wrong with the argument?
options: Nothing: 70 billion weights at 4 bits fit comfortably in 24 GB
The model is published in 16 bits, so 4 bits is 4 times smaller: the frozen weights alone are about 35 GB, before constants, adapters and activations
QLoRA trains in 4-bit arithmetic, which needs extra memory for 4-bit gradients
The factor of 8 is right, but the adapters make the model twice as large

question: A company will serve 12 customer-specific variants of one 7B model from a single GPU, choosing the variant per request. Which training method fits best?
options: Full fine-tuning, because it gives each customer the most freedom
Spectrum, because it trains fewer layers than full fine-tuning
LoRA, kept as 12 separate adapters on one shared base model
Bottleneck adapters, because they also leave the base frozen

question: After training, a teammate reports a validation perplexity of about 1.2 for the router and writes in the release note that the model is excellent, since anything below 10 counts as excellent. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Nothing: a perplexity this close to 1 means the model is almost never unsure, so it routes almost every question correctly
Only the band: a perplexity of 1.2 counts as excellent only for models below one billion parameters

Perplexity is the per-token loss on another scale. Here it averages one or two decisive tokens with many predictable format tokens, and it depends on tokenizer, loss mask and data, so no fixed band applies; the router is judged by routing accuracy and per-answer results
Perplexity should have been computed on the training set, where it is more stable

question: After a month in use, the router has answered 3,000 live questions. To train the next version, a teammate proposes adding all of them to the training data, labelled with the router’s own answers, keeping only those where the top answer was far ahead of the second. What is the best response?
options: Accept: confident answers are almost always right, so the new examples add real-world phrasing at no labelling cost

Decline the labels, keep the questions: the router’s answers would teach it its own mistakes as truth and add no new information; a person labels a sample — close calls and questions asked twice first — and those join the training data, split by family, with the test set unchanged
Accept, but add them to the test set instead of the training data, because live questions are the best test
Decline entirely: live questions must never be used for training

question: A team fine-tunes a vision-language model to read shelf prices from phone photos. Test accuracy is 96 %, yet in the shop the model confidently reports prices for labels that are too blurred to read. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: Too few epochs — train longer so that the model learns to read blurred digits

Neither the training nor the test set held unreadable labels, so the model never learned an ‘unreadable’ answer and the test could not reveal the gap; add such photos with that target to both, and report them as a group of their own
The vision encoder is too small — replace it with CLIP
The LoRA rank is too low — double it

question: Whisper is fine-tuned on 2,000 clips from 40 students, split at random into 90 % training and 10 % test clips. Test WER is 6 %. On recordings from next term’s students it is 19 %. What explains most of the gap?
options: The learning rate was too high, so the model overfitted the training clips
Every test speaker also had clips in training, so the test measured recognition of familiar voices; a test set of held-out speakers would have shown the real error rate
WER on next term’s recordings was computed without normalisation
Whisper is an encoder–decoder model and cannot be fine-tuned on 2,000 clips; a CTC model would generalise better

question: Suppose that in the silver level your labelling rule changes the labels of six test questions and you drop two that lean on an unseen passage. The adapter now scores 0.52 on the repaired test set. Can you write that the repair raised test accuracy from 0.49 to 0.52?
options: Yes: both numbers are test accuracies of the same router
No: the test set itself changed, so the two numbers measure different questions; compare both methods on the repaired test set, once, and report that version as new
Yes, provided the six relabelled questions are excluded from the 0.52
No, because test questions must never be relabelled under any rule

question: A hospital wants a local model to write discharge letters in a fixed five-part layout, using the patient’s current record and the ward’s in-house abbreviations. The record changes daily. A prompted model gets the layout wrong half the time and misuses some abbreviations. Using the lecture, how should the work be split between repairs?
options: Fine-tune on last year’s letters so that the model learns the layout, the abbreviations and the patients’ facts together

Give the facts in the input from the current record, try a schema or complete example letters for the layout first, and consider supervised fine-tuning only for the abbreviations if measured prompts still fail; remove personal data from any training records and score each part of the letter separately
Use retrieval for everything, because a model should never be fine-tuned on medical text
Continue pretraining on the hospital’s records, because the model lacks the domain’s language

question: A team fine-tunes a ticket router through twelve runs and reaches 0.91 validation accuracy against 0.84 for its keyword classifier. They plan to publish 0.91 and ship the merged model in bf16. Which steps from the lecture are missing?
options: None: 0.91 against 0.84 is a clear win on the set used for every choice

Run every method once on a test set kept out of every choice and report counts with their uncertainty; check general requests with the adapter off and on; then score the merged bf16 file on the same questions with the same decision rule, because merging and rounding change the numbers every decision rests on
Retrain once more with a lower learning rate to confirm the result before publishing
Replace the validation set with fresh questions and repeat the twelve runs, then publish the best of them

question: After a release, students begin to ask some questions in Ukrainian, which the generated training data never contained. The share of close calls in the logs doubles. What does the lecture suggest doing first?
options: Retrain at once on machine-translated copies of the training questions

Have a person label a sample of the live Ukrainian questions under the privacy rules, measure the router and the classic classifier on them as a group of their own, and add reviewed real questions to the next dataset, split by family, with a fresh test set
Label the Ukrainian questions with the router’s own answers and add them to the training data
Raise the LoRA rank so that the adapter has room for a second language

question: Suppose a colleague compares two LoRA runs on the router: run A ends with validation loss 0.13 and perplexity 1.14, run B with loss 0.17 and perplexity 1.18 but higher validation accuracy. Which run should be kept for the test, and why?
options: Run A: lower loss and perplexity mean a better model

Run B: the router is judged by the answer it picks, and the loss averages the decisive token with many predictable format tokens and punishes confident mistakes heavily, so it can rise while accuracy improves
Neither: a perplexity above 1.1 shows that both runs failed
Run A, because the loss is computed on more tokens than the accuracy and is therefore more reliable
